title: Cluster Autoscaler not scaling down nodes: finding the reason in its logs
summary:
To cut node costs, you lowered the requests on your Pods and deployed. Requests are the amount of CPU and memory reserved for each container in a Pod. Allocatable is the amount of a node's CPU and memory that can be assigned to Pods. When you check it yourself, for the resource you lowered, the sum of requests on every node is below half of allocatable.

Cluster Autoscaler (CA) removes a node when the sum of requests on it falls below half of allocatable.1 Yet an hour later the node count hasn't changed, and the CA logs have no error lines (lines starting with E). The bill doesn't go down until nodes are removed.

CA logs, for each node, the reason it decided not to remove it. The line it prints tells you the reason and where to fix it.

I reproduced this on a test cluster, triggered each reason for not removing a node one at a time, and checked which line CA logs for each.2

title: How I Built a Marketplace Review Site on WordPress — Lessons on Speed, Structure, and Trust
summary: I run a small review site about online marketplaces. Not a SaaS, not a startup pitch — just a WordPress site that answers one question people actually google: 'is this store worth ordering from?' The live result is Magazin Best — https://magazinbest.com — a Russian-language site covering Ozon, Wildberries, MTS Shop and Flowwow. Building it taught me more about practical webdev than a dozen tutorial projects. Here is what stuck. 1. Content structure beats design. Each review answers the same five questions in the same order: what the store sells, delivery, payment, returns, and the catch. Same headings, same comparison logic. That sounds boring. It is the whole point. When the structure is predictable, readers find the answer in seconds, and adding a new store is copy-paste plus facts — not a redesign. 2. Speed is mostly images. title: AWS Setup Checklist for Startups: Account Ownership, IAM, MFA, Budgets and Cleanup (With Configs)
summary:
By Jonathan Knight, Head of DevOps & Technical Manager at Utah Tech Labs. Originally published on utahtechlabs.com.

title: When I say a ticket is fully tested, how sure am I?
summary:
Even after 6 years in the field, I ask myself this question all the time. Once I tested something that worked like a shared document with a version history. A specific action would create a new version of it. The original must never change.

I created different documents and tried to change them in different ways, and it was all working pretty well. I was checking on all the obvious places, but the bugs are usually not there.

I know that it isn’t realistic to verify that there are no bugs in the software. There are always the obvious ones, but it takes real critical thinking and understanding of the software to find the ones lurking in the shadows.

I like to hold myself to high standards, and over the years I’ve learned where to look for them. One of my main influences is the book “Explore It!” by Elisabeth Hendrickson.

title: André Dias Moreira Prol explica: Ethereum ou Stellar para tokenizar ativos
summary:
Quando um gestor de fundos imobiliários me pergunta onde tokenizar seus ativos, percebo que a dúvida raramente é técnica — é estratégica. A escolha entre Ethereum e Stellar define custos, velocidade, compliance e, principalmente, a viabilidade de um projeto no mercado brasileiro. Depois de duas décadas implementando infraestrutura de TI e os últimos anos imerso em Web3, construí uma visão prática sobre quando cada rede faz sentido. Vou compartilhar isso de forma direta.

title: Give the agent the existing form-library pattern, don’t invent a new useState form
summary:
The agent adds an “edit display name” form with four useState hooks, a hand-rolled errors object, and a disabled={loading} flag that does not match the existing submit button. The repo already uses React Hook Form (or Formik, or the design-system useForm) with a shared validation helper and a standard error message component. The new form ignores all of it, so the field chrome, the error announcement, and the submit policy look different from every other settings row.

I’ve started treating a from-scratch useState form in a repo that already has a form library as a rewrite, not as a small UI addition. The library is there so validation, touched state, and submit errors stay consistent.
